- create "agent" appServer skeleton, maintaining the agent.db SQLite database, this appServer maintains all state, broadcast that state to its clients.

- create "shell/js/workBench.js" element skeleton, the top level visual container, taking 100% of the app-space below the face-shells titlebar

- create "shell/js/tabContainer" element skeleton, an element with one row for tabs at the top, displaying the tab content in the remaining vertical space.

- create a test/ folder for both "agent" components, face-app and appServer, as well as a test/ folder for both new shell elements, these four test/ folders will the ONLY test containers for this app.

- this is the hello-word item for this goal.

# DECIDED

The agent app
- The workBench lays out the agent face app: three panes, a vertical tool strip on each side; the app loads on the face, on loopback and through a relay.
- No agents talk to each other in this app (Q1): each agent is the only agent and user of its node (goal/G3.1); a break of it is a red Q.
- Left tool: relay-state/shell/agent/config.json, whether the title bar shows the server's DEBUG state; the title shows the bug icon while it is on and the server is in DEBUG.
- Right tool: the agent server's DEBUG state. The app requires the agent family through spirit and calls debug {on} (Q3, Q5); the server keeps it in relay-state/process/agent/config.json across restarts, the one its built-in DEBUG verb switches (Q4); the page reads it only from the stream, from the moment it opens.
- The move into shell/ and the loading tree are goal/G41.3's (Q5 there).

Where an app runs and shows
- A node's sidecars are its own state, at the mirror of its app's path: relay-state/shell/<app>/<app>.js.sidecar.json, relay-state/process/<name>/<name>.js.sidecar.json. Out of git; no sidecar beside the code is tracked or counts.
- Every fs.annotate writes the face part there, the node's door as the face link (Q10, Q11: no compatibility with the old shell; its client part is gone).
- Intrinsic is a coded list, INTRINSIC in spirit/run/spirit/coreFiles.js, the development team's, changed under Andy's grant. The commit check, the node starting servers and every face part ask it; no manifest or sidecar says it.
- A new node runs and shows its intrinsic apps only (minimal == intrinsic); each node ticks the rest once.
- A server runs while it is intrinsic or its node's sidecar says home: true. relay-state/node.json's servers section and the manifests' runs are gone (Q6, Q7: no central list).
- The node starts or stops a server, and streams an app's face part (an app-face job), as its sidecar changes; every appServer's status reaches the face too.

The face and the Apps app
- shell/js/appInstaller.js: one activate/deactivate button, one state wherever drawn; it proposes and draws only what the node answers or the stream says (rule/19). A shell app's button switches its face mark; a server's its home, and with it every app that names that server. Intrinsic apps and Apps itself have no button.
- Apps lists standalone shell apps and appServers only, with an installer column, an installable-only filter, and a details panel with no checkbox (intrinsic said in words).
- The face (shell/boot.js) shows an app while its face mark is on or it is intrinsic, and, if it names a server, while that server runs (goal/G27.16); otherwise its icon goes and its open pages close. An intrinsic app with no face part takes its name and icon from its manifest; Join stays boot's.
- Only the new face shell is served; the old home shell is not kept compatible.

# FILES

- process/js/agent/ (agent.js, agent.json, agent.family/api.js), shell/agent/ (agent.js, agent.json), shell/js/workBench.js, shell/js/tabContainer.js, shell/js/appInstaller.js, shell/apps/apps.js, shell/boot.js, shell/js/textViewer.js, shell/js/fileViewer.js
- spirit/run/spirit/: coreFiles.js, fileSystem.js, jobs.js, faceHome.js, server.js, kernel.js, introSpector.js, nodeSettings.js; every app manifest (runs and intrinsic gone)

# TESTS

- product tests: process/js/agent/test, shell/agent/test, shell/js/test (workBench, tabContainer, appInstaller), shell/apps/test, shell/test/boot
- suites: spirit/test/serverHomeSidecar.js, spirit/test/faceAnnotations.js

# OPEN

- Intrinsic apps built for the old shell only (Grants, Group Manager, introSpector, Jobs, Relay Monitor, Rotate Key, Stats) now show on the face and may not open there.
- The tag: every node and relay that takes it runs and shows only its intrinsic apps until ticked.

FACE/ MOVES INTO SHELL/

THE MOVE
- face/shell.js becomes shell/boot.js.

WHAT CHANGES WITH IT
- spirit.js loads shell/boot.js where it loaded face/shell.js.
- face.html links /shell/face.css and /shell/favicon.svg.
- The relay serves the face from its map of addresses to files (relayServer.js, FACE_FILES): the map names the new addresses and the moved files, and the old addresses are gone. The relays run the new code the same day as the nodes (no backward compatibility before alpha). relayServer.js is the bones: a team review.
- shell/boot.js names its own parts by their new paths (the seal, the login app).
- Login and Join are the two mandatory components of shell/boot.js, one for its loopback mode and one for its face mode (Andy). boot makes hard-coded assumptions about both and disregards their sidecars.
- Both apps are core whole, so no page can change them: the node's file gate refuses every core file. Today only join.js is core.
- login.json and join.json are no manifests: they are code, the apps' own UI text (their steps), and stay beside their apps as they are, core with them (Andy, Q9: "if they're code, just keep them, they are obviously NOT manifests."). Nothing of either app is deleted.
- coreFiles.js keeps them core: shell/boot.js, shell/seal.js, shell/face.css, shell/favicon.svg and shell/login/, as face/ was.
- The tests that name the old paths follow: spirit/run/test/spirit.js and the throwaway red.

WHAT BOOT LOADS (Andy)
- shell/boot.js boots only itself and the home and Join components it needs, as they stand. That is the only preload allowed.
- Every face app loads its own components, as a tree, through spirit.require, each once. No core component knows about an application.
- spirit.require de-dupes, as node's require does (Andy): a path required twice is fetched and run once, and every caller gets the same answer; a script the boot already loaded counts as required. Today on a page it fetches and runs the file on every call.

THE CACHE (Andy, Q2)
- spirit.js loads the cache itself (shell/js/spiritData.js) when its client part starts, on a page and in a process alike, and keeps every streamed dataset, each type through its own translator, which its type loads. The file tree is cached too, by the files type's translator (Andy: "Q2, the file tree must be cached."). Not kept: stats and presence, which are display streams.
- A page's cache has no cap; a process's cache is a node store, so it sheds oldest first past a byte cap.
- On a reconnect a cache forgets what it kept, and its partner pushes it whole again, for every type.
- One write: the cache takes a change only when the owner's acceptance comes back on the stream, never a local copy first (rule/19).
- The translators are lazy too (Andy, Q4): every app adds its own data, tables and searches to the cache when it loads, its translator with it. A type loaded late is handed its data whole by its partner when it subscribes.

- i already know i need the following tables for a primitive version, 

- a provider table. keyed by ID same as the shadow-roll (with Label and Description, URL, and API_KEY)
- a persona table.  keyed by ID same as the shadow-roll  (with Label and Description, and a codeMirror-field for the persona-description i give it with every prompt)
- a jobs table.  keyed by ID same as the shadow-roll (with Label and Description, boolean loop-flag (not for the model, for the agent-app), and a codeMirror-field for the job-description that may come with a prompt)

- the the ID as key for all tables comes from the idea, that when i give an agent node-api's as tools, i may want to control access using the same grants-app as i use for peers. this has a bunch of holes, because, i'd have to put my "personas" OR "jobs" into the shadow roll....

# keys (Andy, Q1 and Q2: "they WILL need grants and i want keys that are separate from a label", "we'll put off the grant-problem, but not the keys.")

- every row of the three tables (providers, personas, jobs) has a key of its own, a peer's shape: a key pair the agent server makes when the row is created. The public half is the row's id; its label is a separate caption that may change.
- the private half never leaves the agent server, nor does a provider's API key: a page sets one, and only sees whether it is set.
- grants are put off: how a row's key is granted node verbs (the shadow roll, or the grants app reading the agent server) is decided when tools come.

# out of scope for now

- a conversation context. The primitive version sends a job's persona and job text fresh with each call. The direction for later (Andy): ONE context, persisted and maintained, for each persona (its direct chat) and for each job; each kept within a probabilityBucket-style limit by built-in shedding strategies, possibly in layers, an overall bucket over component buckets. The node's traffic log does not record model calls: they are plain web requests, not peer packets.

chat.text:
- cw: 1. Yes. The model keeps nothing between calls. Every request carries the whole conversation it should know: the system prompt, the message history, any files or tool results. It knows the last prompt only because the caller sends it again. That holds for the Anthropic and OpenAI chat APIs, and for a local model run through unsloth.
- Two caveats, neither of them memory:
  - Some providers can keep the history for you on their side (OpenAI's stored conversations, for example). That is still history sent back in, just held by them, under an id you pass.
  - Prompt caching (Anthropic, OpenAI, a local KV cache) only makes a repeated prefix cheaper and faster; it changes nothing the model knows.
- 2. Yes. Two personas can take turns on the same provider, the same key, even the same model, each with its own system prompt and its own history. As long as you never mix the two message lists, neither sees the other.
- What they share is only the plumbing: rate limits and spend on the key, and on a local box the GPU and its memory.
- That is how an agent app can run several agents on one model: each is just its own list of messages.
does it not also mean that i could have multiple model-providers open at the same time, and hand each completely unrelated tasks?

- cw: yes. Each call is self-contained, so nothing ties a task to one provider. You can have Anthropic, OpenAI and a local model working at the same moment, each on its own task with its own history, in parallel.
- What it takes is only bookkeeping on your side: which history belongs to which task, which key or endpoint each uses, and the different request formats, which an adapter per provider hides.
- The one real difference between them is the model itself: what each is good at, its context size, its price. You can even hand the same history from one provider to another mid-task, since it is just your list of messages.

- Feedback on the box, one point each:
- Providers: the API key must never leave the agent server. It streams its state to its pages, so the key column is write-only: a page sets it, and only ever sees set or not set. A provider also needs its API kind (Anthropic, OpenAI, or OpenAI-compatible for a local model) and a model name, beside the URL.
- Personas: as written, the persona text is the system prompt, sent with every call. Fits.
- Jobs: missing is what a job runs on, its persona and its provider. And its history: from your own question earlier, a job's train of context is its list of messages, kept here. That table, messages by job, will be the bulk of agent.db.
- Size: a CodeMirror field can outgrow one packet, so the tables reach pages through bounded searches and per-row reads, never as one dump.
- The left-edge icons: each opens its table as a tab in the middle pane. That is the workBench tool strip plus tabContainer, as built.
- IDs: the holes you name are real. Personas and jobs are no peers, and putting them in the shadow roll muddles it. Grants only matter once an agent gets node verbs as tools, which no table here needs yet.

Q1: Start with plain local ids for the three tables, and give personas keys of their own only when tools need grants?

why? the WILL need grants and i want keys that are separate from a label...

explain?

- cw: my reason was only to put off the shadow-roll problem. If they will need grants, keys from the start are better: nothing to migrate later.
- So each row gets a key of its own, the same shape as a peer's: a key pair the agent server makes when the row is created. The public half is the id; the label stays a separate, changeable caption, as a contact's does.
- Why a key pair and not just a random id: to use node verbs under a grant, the agent must sign its requests as that key, as a peer does. So the agent server keeps the private half, and it never leaves it, like the API key.
- The hole you named stays one decision: the grants app picks whom to grant from the shadow roll. Either agent keys get rows there, marked as agents, or the grants app also reads the agent server.
- One more choice first: who acts, and so needs the key.

we'll put off the grant-problem, but not the keys.

- cw: boxed: a key pair for every row of the three tables, the public half its id, the label separate; private halves and API keys never leave the agent server; grants put off.
- Still open from my feedback: a job's persona and provider, and its history table. Shall I put them in the box?
why a history table? if at all, it's most certainly deferred, the node allready creates history for every api call, doesn't it?

- cw: not for this. The node's traffic log records packets to and from peers. A call from the agent server to a model provider is a plain web request, and nothing records it today.
- Why I named it: from your question about providers, the model remembers nothing, so a job that talks back and forth must send its whole conversation every call. That conversation has to live somewhere, and it is the job's.
- But for a primitive version it can wait: a job that sends its persona and its job text fresh each time needs no history at all. Deferred, then: I box it as out of scope for now.
